In physics, '''Landau–de Gennes theory''' describes the NI transition, i.e., phase transition between nematic [[liquid crystals]] and isotropic liquids, which is based on the classical [[Landau theory|Landau's theory]] and was developed by [[Pierre-Gilles de Gennes]] in 1969.<ref>De Gennes, P. G. (1969). Phenomenology of short-range-order effects in the isotropic phase of nematic materials. Physics Letters A, 30 (8), 454-455.</ref><ref>De Gennes, P. (1971). Short range order effects in the isotropic phase of nematics and cholesterics. Molecular Crystals and Liquid Crystals, 12(3), 193-214.</ref> The phenomenological theory uses the [[Q tensor|<math>\mathbf{Q}</math> tensor]] as an [[order parameter]] in expanding the [[Helmholtz free energy|free energy]] density.<ref>De Gennes, P. G., & Prost, J. (1993). The physics of liquid crystals (No. 83). Oxford university press.</ref><ref>Mottram, N. J., & Newton, C. J. (2014). Introduction to Q-tensor theory. arXiv preprint arXiv:1409.3542.</ref>

==Mathematical description==
The NI transition is a first-order phase transition, albeit it is very weak. The order parameter is the <math>\mathbf{Q}</math> tensor, which is symmetric, traceless, second-order tensor and vanishes in the isotropic liquid phase. We shall consider a uniaxial <math>\mathbf Q</math> tensor, which is defined by

:<math>\mathbf Q = S(\mathbf n\otimes\mathbf n - \tfrac{1}{3}\mathbf I)</math>

where <math>S=S(T)</math> is the scalar order parameter and <math>\mathbf n</math> is the director. The <math>\mathbf Q</math> tensor is zero in the isotropic liquid phase since the scalar order parameter <math>S</math> is zero, but becomes non-zero in the nematic phase.

Near the NI transition, the ([[Helmholtz free energy|Helmholtz]] or [[Gibbs free energy|Gibbs]]) free energy density <math>\mathcal{F}</math> is expanded about as

:<math>\mathcal{F} = \mathcal{F}_0 + \frac{A}{2} Q_{ij}Q_{ji} - \frac{B}{3} Q_{ij}Q_{jk}Q_{ki} + \frac{C}{4} (Q_{ij}Q_{ij})^2 </math>

or more compactly

:<math>\mathcal{F} = \mathcal{F}_0 + \frac{A}{2}\mathrm{tr} \,\mathbf{Q}^2 -  \frac{B}{3}\mathrm{tr} \,\mathbf{Q}^3 + \frac{C}{4}(\mathrm{tr} \,\mathbf{Q}^2)^2</math>

where <math>(A,B,C)</math> are functions of temperature. Near the phase transition, we can expand <math>A(T)=a (T-T_*)+\cdots</math>, <math>B(T) = b + \cdots</math> and <math>C(T)=c + \cdots</math> with <math>(a,b,c)</math> being three positive constants. Now substituting the <math>\mathbf Q</math> tensor results in<ref>Kleman, M., & Lavrentovich, O. D. (Eds.). (2003). Soft matter physics: an introduction. New York, NY: Springer New York.</ref>

:<math>\mathcal{F} - \mathcal{F}_0 = \frac{a}{3}(T-T_*)S^2  - \frac{2b}{27} S^3 + \frac{c}{9}S^4.</math>

This is minimized when

:<math>3a(T-T_*) S - b S^2 + 2c S^3=0.</math>

The two required solutions of this equation are

:<math>\begin{align}\text{Isotropic:} & \,\,S_I = 0,\\
\text{Nematic:} & \,\,S_N = \frac{b}{4c} \left[1+\sqrt{1-\frac{24ac}{b^2}(T-T_*)}\,\right]>0.
\end{align}</math>

The NI transition temperature <math>T_{NI}</math>  is not simply equal to <math>T_*</math> (which would be the case in second-order phase transition), but is given by

:<math>T_{NI} = T_* + \frac{b^2}{27ac}, \quad S_{NI} = \frac{b}{3c}</math>

<math>S_{NI}</math> is the scalar order parameter at the transition.
